newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr shoved aside by surging yen.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr shoved aside by surging yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar was shoved to the sidelines at a nervous midsession as the yen stormed to year highs on a host of currencies while the U.S. dollar dived.

The latter shed 1-1/2 yen to hit 114.00 on a corrosive mix of speculation the Federal Reserve would not in fact tighten at its policy meeting today but Japan could soon be raising its rates. Traders said massive stop loss sales were triggered with a break of 114.70 and the panic spilled over into AUD/yen which tumbled to 88.18/28 yen from 89.42/52 at the opening.
AUD/U$ was ignored amid all this mayhem and dealers looked for it to idle above key US$0.7720 support for now.

By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar was keeping its head down at US$0.7730/35 having backed off from an early test of US$0.7750. That was down on Monday's late US$0.7745/50 but still above its offshore trough of US$0.7725.
On the crosses the currency crumbled to its lowest level on the yen since mid-November last year, bringing its losses to a spectacular 12 percent since peaking just above 100.00 on May 1.

In the same period the U.S. dollar had collapsed to under 114.00 yen from 127.45 and left the market -- which had been hugely long of US$ -- traumatised. And dealers saw more pain ahead unless the Fed hiked U.S. rates tonight.
Market opinion has swung from being reasonably confident the Fed would tighten to utter uncertainty as U.S. inflation stayed low and some key growth indicators slowed of their own accord.
Whatever the decision it would have conflicting implications for the local currency.

For one thing a hike should help US$/yen rally which in turn would drag AUD/yen up with it, but it would also narrow the A$'s official interest differential over the U.S. unit to just 25 basis points.
On the other hand a U.S. hike might be seen as reducing the risk of a cut in Australian rates, to the benefit of the A$.
The last time domestic rates were below those in the U.S. was in the early 1980's but a 0.25 point Fed hike and a 0.5 point cut here, would do just that.

Analysts were unsure how offshore investors would react to such a scenario but suspected the local dollar could take a beating while they got used to the novelty. Some felt the RBA would be reluctant to risk such a slide given that the strength of the dollar had played a major part in bringing Australian inflation down.
But, equally, if the Fed stayed silent tonight it could be seen as a window of opportunity for one more RBA easing.
Analysts said it was pretty clear from political rhetoric after the 1997/98 budget last week that the government was looking for the RBA to cut again.

Indeed, there were rumours the Treasury had asked for an easing at the last RBA board meeting but the bank had declined because of rising wages growth. Treasury was thought to have argued, as do some market economists, that aggregate wages data overstate the danger and key figures this week will show private sector deals were resonably subdued.
The Department of Industrial Relations releases its Q1 report on enterprise bargains on Wednesday.
The Q4 report showed wage growth in the private sector slowed to 4.4 percent from 5.3 percent in Q3, and for all sectors to 4.4 percent from 4.8 percent.
Some were counting on a further slowdown, although a survey by HSBC Markets released Monday suggested the pace of wage deals may have actually picked up a little in Q1.

The first quarter data on average weekly earnings had indeed showed a surprisingly strong rise to an annual 4.6 percent, but there was an argument this had been biased upwards by the public sector and detailed data on Thursday would show the private sector was not at fault. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
